entries.title: UK: Two Latvian men arrested for breaking into RAF base
entries.summary: The men were arrested for breaching a perimeter fence at a UK air base that houses US and NATO intelligence operations. The incident comes after an alleged terror plot at another air base in England was foiled recently.
entries.content:
October 9, 2026

The men were arrested for breaching a perimeter fence at a UK air base that houses US and NATO intelligence operations. The incident comes after an alleged terror plot at another air base in England was foiled recently.

Two Latvian men have been arrested for breaching the perimeter fence at an RAF base used by the US military, UK police said Thursday.

The two UK residents, aged 36 and 32, were arrested by counterterrorism police at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in southeastern England, 70 miles north of London.

Police said they were being held on suspicion of trespassing, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the UK."

A former World War II airbase, RAF Molesworth, is now a non-flying facility that is managed by the US Air Force.

It houses intelligence personnel from US Africa Command and the NATO Intelligence Fusion Center, which provides information to the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe.

The incident comes after several men were arrested amid an alleged terror plot at another UK air base last month.

What do we know about the incident at RAF Molesworth?

According to a statement from Counter Terrorism Policing London, officers from the Ministry of Defense Police and Cambridgeshire Constabulary began investigating an incident at approximately 10 p.m. local time on Wednesday after an abandoned vehicle was found near the edge of the base.

Police later discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence and arrested the two suspects at around 2 a.m. on Thursday.

The men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage. They were later arrested on charges of entering a prohibited place with the intent to harm the UK.

Both men remain in police custody. Due to the nature of the offense, the matter is being investigated by counterterrorism police.

Is this related to the RAF Fairford incident?

On September 27, authorities discovered three suspicious vans near RAF Fairford, a British air base from which US bombers launched strikes against Iran. This triggered a widespread investigation that led to seven arrests.

Last weekend, the US Air Force brought home all the bombers deployed to the base.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of the counterterrorism unit, said that while UK authorities are "very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites", there is "nothing to suggest" the incident at RAF Molesworth is related to what happened at RAF Fairford last week, although she added that the investigation was still in its "very early stages."

The US European Command acknowledged the incident but declined to comment on specific force protection measures.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Afghan women facing arrest for dress code violations: UN
entries.summary: In recent months, the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan have arrested or detained dozens of women for alleged violations of dress codes and for appearing in public without a male guardian.
entries.content:
October 8, 2026

In recent months, the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan have arrested or detained dozens of women for alleged violations of dress codes and for appearing in public without a male guardian.

At least 52 women and one girl were arrested or detained in the Afghan cities of Herat and Kabul between July and September of 2026, according to a statement released by the United Nations on Thursday.

"Women were detained for not wearing a chador [an all-enveloping, cloak-like garment], having visible hair, wearing colourful scarves or makeup, or being in public without a mahram [male chaperone]," the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said.

According to the mission, the detained women were released after being held for several hours. It also warned that the number of cases could be higher due to underreporting.

UNAMA said it was "gravely concerned" by the arrests, detentions, and threats of arrest.

The mission stated that the detentions violate women's and girls' rights to freedom of movement, expression, and autonomy. The detentions also expose them to severe social stigma in traditional Afghan society, UNAMA said.

In June, Afghan authorities opened fire on a rare protest in Herat over the arrests and detentions of women for alleged dress code violations. According to witnesses and the UN mission, at least one person was killed and several others were injured.

What restrictions do women in Afghanistan face?

Since seizing power in 2021 as US-led forces withdrew from Afghanistan, the Taliban government has imposed severe restrictions on women and girls, including banning them from attending school beyond the primary level and limiting what they can wear and where they can go.

In public, women must wear a full hijab, which includes a headscarf, a long robe that covers the body, and a face covering. The Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice enforces these rules.

Earlier this week, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued four arrest warrants for senior Taliban officials, accusing them of committing crimes against humanity by systematically depriving women and girls in Afghanistan of their rights.

Hovewer, the Taliban rejected the decision, calling it a politically motivated violation of Afghanistan's sovereignty.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: US suspends Microsoft, Adobe from filing for green cards
entries.summary: The Trump administration cut off tech firms, including Microsoft and Adobe, from filing for green cards for their foreign workers.
entries.content:
United States of America

US suspends Microsoft, Adobe from filing for green cards

October 8, 2026

The Trump administration cut off tech firms, including Microsoft and Adobe, from filing for green cards for their foreign workers.

The Trump administration on Thursday said it was suspending major tech firms, including Microsoft, from applying for a program that allowed their foreign workers to work permanently in the US.

US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling accused those tech firms of abusing the program — the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) — that had so far been a legal pathway for workers to apply for green cards.

"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said.

Sonderling said the suspensions were due to ongoing federal investigations into those firms.

There are good reasons that Indian media firms covered the issue so urgently because many of those firms are either Indian or rely on thousands of Indian professionals who've moved to the country.

Trump administration accuses Microsoft of abusing program for green cards

Vice President JD Vance said the PERM system required companies to advertise work in the US before they applied for green cards for foreign workers due to a lack of qualified American job applicants.

"They'll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They'll go out there and say that 'We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.' And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants," Vance claimed.

"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.

The announcement came hours before US President Donald Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

Microsoft says majority of its workers are Americans

Microsoft said in a statement that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information, saying the majority of its workers are Americans and that a large part of the H-1B filings have to do with the status of people already based in the US.

"We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings," the company said.

The H-1B visa program is another part of the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration, as concerns have long persisted that the visa for skilled workers has displaced Americans in favor of lower-cost foreign labor.

Microsoft employs 125,000 US workers and 103,000 international workers, according to the company's 2025 annual report.

entries.title: South Africa: Anti-migrant protests turn violent
entries.summary: A court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications reignited violent protests against immigration in South Africa.
entries.content:
South Africa

South Africa: Anti-migrant protests turn violent

October 8, 2026

A court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications reignited violent protests against immigration in South Africa.

Anti-migrant protests erupted in South Africa on Thursday as tensions over immigration were reignited by a court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications.

Some of the protests turned violent, according to local media reports. This included incidents in the coastal city of Durban and the Soweto township of Johannesburg, where cars were set on fire and gunshots were heard.

What do we know about protests in South Africa?

The unrest in Durban reportedly followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee center stop processing asylum applications. About 10 vehicles were overturned and set on fire. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.

Meanwhile, in Soweto, residents clashed with foreign shop owners, and gunshots were heard, according to the broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.

At least nine vehicles were torched, said Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department spokesman Superintendent Xolani Fihla in an interview with SABC television.

"It's reported that there were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," he said. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported."

What has the court decided?

The court ruling that sparked the flare-up of xenophobic tensions deemed certain provisions of the government's refugee policy to be unconstitutional.

The court explained that this was because the provisions prevented individuals from accessing the asylum system on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.

Recently, this ruling has led hundreds of people, reportedly including those who do not qualify for asylum, to flock to government refugee centers.

On Wednesday, the government emphasized that the judgement "does not grant refugee status or permanent residence automatically to anyone who enters South Africa."

Xenophobic sentiment in South Africa

South Africa has experienced months of anti-immigrant protests this year. Populist and anti-immigrant groups have demanded that undocumented foreign nationals leave by June 30.

Amidst international criticism, tens of thousands of people have fled the country, while some were repatriated by their governments.

Although South Africa has a third of its population unemployed, it remains the largest economy in Africa and continues to attract migrants.

Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fueling crime, and straining public services. However, social scientists have said these accusations are not supported by evidence.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: US will not resume strikes on Iran before midterms — Trump
entries.summary: President Donald Trump said the US will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterm elections on November 3. High gas and grocery prices are top concerns for voters.
entries.content:
Iran

US will not resume strikes on Iran before midterms — Trump

October 8, 2026

President Donald Trump said the US will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterm elections on November 3. High gas and grocery prices are top concerns for voters.

US President Donald Trump said he will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.

Trump's announcement on social media on Thursday came after two US media outlets reported that he was weighing options to strike Iran.

The Atlantic magazine reported  that the thinking was Trump would want to maintain the period of relative calm in the war with Iran until after the elections to keep the deeply unpopular war out of the news. The US has not struck the country in recent weeks.

A Pentagon official told Axios that the Department of Defense's job was to be ready for possible strikes on Iran if the president ordered them.

Iran war, gas prices, and US midterms: What to know

The US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire agreement in April, but that agreement didn't hold as both countries resumed fighting in the months that followed.

Trump said at the UN General Assembly that he could yet escalate the war with Iran.

But gas and fuel prices remain high in the US, with many voters already feeling the pressure of high prices for groceries and other goods — factors that have weighed on candidates in Trump's Republican Party.

Plus, the economy remains one of the top concerns for voters this midterm, when US citizens are going to be electing members of Congress.

In his social media post on Thursday, Trump also said his team has been "having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran."

That came after Trump, at the end of September, publicly rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — the vital waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil once flowed — to commercial shipping if the US met necessary conditions.

Then Iran last week said it had received a counterproposal.

Pentagon deploys more resources to the Middle East, WSJ reports

Trump's post also came as the military dispatched more resources to the Middle East, according to a report the Wall Street Journal.

US officials said a third aircraft-carrier strike group, and its thousands of troops, would arrive by the end of November, according to the newspaper.

entries.title: France: Police clash with protesters at Paris student rally
entries.summary: Police fired tear gas at protesters in Paris again as students continue to voice grievances about school conditions across France. The education minister has said 3,000 substitute teachers will reach schools soon.
entries.content:
France

France: Police clash with protesters at Paris student rally

October 8, 2026

Police fired tear gas at protesters in Paris again as students continue to voice grievances about school conditions across France. The education minister has said 3,000 substitute teachers will reach schools soon.

Thousands of students demonstrated near Bastille Square in Paris on Thursday afternoon, as France's nationwide student protests continue.

Crowds of students climbed the famous Bastille Monument. Some waved the French flag and sang the national anthem.

Footage from Reuters TV showed riot police charging at protesters with batons as they moved in to clear the square.

Across France, some 71,500 people took part in Thursday's protests and police detained more than 500, the Interior Ministry said.

France will send 3,000 substitute teachers "within the next hours" to struggling high schools, the education minister said Thursday.

"Within the next hours, 3,000 teachers will be joining these institutions," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told the evening news on the TF1 television channel.

Geffray said they would be at schools between Friday to Tuesday.

Students barricade high school

Earlier on Thursday, students barricaded Helene Boucher High School in northeastern Paris with trash bins before police broke up the protest with tear gas.

As students gathered at the school, riot police assembled in the side streets. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid identification.

The school has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital and was one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protests on Thursday.

Although the rallies have largely been peaceful, some demonstrators have set fires and vandalized bus shelters.

In response, the police have used tear gas, batons, and blast balls. Human rights groups and children accuse officers of using excessive force.

Following an incident in which a teenager's hand was blown off, the government suspended the use of stun grenades for crowd control on Wednesday.

Since late September, when students, most of whom are under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, police have made more than 6,600 arrests, according to the Interior Ministry.

Government promises response

On Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised that the government would present "concrete, quick, and fully funded responses" to the protests by the end of October.

Nevertheless, student protest leaders said this was not good enough and called for more marches.

In a televised address, Lecornu also lamented the "violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalized, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults."

entries.title: US prosecutors add new torture charge against Maduro
entries.summary: US prosecutors have added a new charge to their case against deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing the couple of conspiring to commit torture.
entries.content:
Venezuela

US prosecutors add new torture charge against Maduro

October 8, 2026

US prosecutors have added a new charge to their case against deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing the couple of conspiring to commit torture.

US prosecutors have announced new charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents and US citizens.

The new charges against the couple are in addition to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced, according to a revised indictment released Thursday.

Both Maduro and Flores have denied the previous charges brought against them.

Maduro's lawyer Barry Pollack said in a statement, "President Maduro denies the charges in the new indictment and looks ​forward to his day ‌in court."

Revised indictment adds pressure on Maduro

The revised indictment alleged that the couple committed human rights violations as part of a scheme to hold on to power.

High tensions between the US and a socialist and oil-rich Venezuela were a constant during Maduro's 13 years in power.

Human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but Thursday's indictment marks the first time that Maduro could be held to account over the allegations.

"He authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition," the indictment said.

The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest.

Maduro's wife seeks release from New York jail

Meanwhile, the 69-year-old Flores is due in Manhattan federal court on Thursday. She is expected to ask a judge to release her from jail and place her under house arrest, citing health problems.

Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds (11.4 kilograms) in custody, suffers from dizziness and shortness of breath and may have suffered a minor heart attack in July.

They have proposed that she live at a New York residence under 24-hour security.

Prosecutors, however, oppose the request, arguing that Flores poses an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released.

They said she has received hospital treatment when necessary while in custody.

Trump vs. Maduro

Maduro, 63, and Flores are being held at a federal detention center in Brooklyn as they await their trial in June next year.

The couple was captured during an unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid on their Caracas home on January 3, which was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation."

Critics have accused Trump of operating outside international law.

They were subsequently brought to New York, where they face existing drug trafficking and firearms charges.

Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Meanwhile, in August, Trump announced that the US had reached a deal to take control of part of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, which Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez also termed "historic."

entries.title: EU pulls sponsorship from Disinfo2026 event in Lithuania
entries.summary: The EU's diplomatic service, Canada and host nation Lithuania all pulled support from a disinformation event in Vilnius. Amid reports of US pressure, the EU said it was "uncomfortable with the framing" of some panels.
entries.content:
Lithuania

EU pulls sponsorship from disinformation event in Lithuania

October 8, 2026

The EU's diplomatic service, Canada and host nation Lithuania all pulled support from a disinformation event in Vilnius. Amid reports of US pressure, the EU said it was "uncomfortable with the framing" of some panels.

The European Union on Thursday offered its reasons for withdrawing sponsorship for a disinformation event in Lithuania, following media reports claiming that it did so after pressure from the US government. 

The EU's foreign affairs division, the European External Action Service (EEAS), and the governments of Canada and Lithuania all pulled their support from the event at short notice. Sponsors' logos on flyers and placards at the event were hastily covered over with paper strips. 

They withdrew participation in Disinfo2026 after pressure from the US State Department, according to reports in several media outlets, including the British newspaper The Guardian.

What did the EU say about its decision?

EU spokesperson Christian Wigand made no mention of the US or external pressure on Thursday but also did not repudiate the reports.

"We were not comfortable with the framing of some of the discussions at the event," he told reporters in Brussels.

"The organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU," he said.

He refused to discuss details of which discussions or what framing had perturbed the EEAS. He also would not comment on whether there had been talks with US officials on the matter.

"I'm not commenting on diplomatic exchanges as a matter of principle," he said.

What signs of potential controversy at Disinfo2026 were visible?

While a number of the sessions planned on the event's website across two days at the Radisson Blu Lietuva Hotel in Vilnius appeared to have the potential to perturb more sensitive members of Donald Trump's administration, the opening two sessions on Wednesday morning stood out. 

The opening of the conference was an interview with Kimberly Prost, a judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has come under sustained and heavy fire from Trump and his administration during his second term. 

This was followed by an hourlong session entitled "USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back," using the acronym for Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference. One of the planned speakers was a former CIA officer.

Strong US free speech safeguards in the First Amendment to its Constitution mean the US has maintained a comparatively hands-off approach to combating disinformation — both in the political and legal spheres. This has arguably intensified, however, under President Donald Trump's leadership, with critics alleging it's partly because of his own often uneasy relationship with the truth.

entries.title: How the Houthi-Saudi conflict is affecting countries on Africa's Red Sea coast — and beyond
entries.summary: The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which Yemeni government forces are trying to take back from the Houthis, is located not far from Djibouti and other African states.
entries.content:
Africa

How the Houthi-Saudi conflict is affecting African countries

October 8, 2026

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which Yemeni government forces are trying to take back from the Houthis, is located not far from Djibouti and other African states.

In September, one of the major conflicts in the Middle East came within sight of Africa, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels captured Yemen's Perim Island. 

The island forms the narrowest point of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the southern entrance of the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It is roughly 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Djibouti and 20-minutes by air to Ethiopia.

In early October, Yemen's armed forces and their Saudi allies launched a counteroffensive. TheIran-backed Houthis have been firing on merchant ships since the start of the Gaza war in 2023. 

The economic consequences for Africa is coupled with a refugee inflow

African economies are already suffering from crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, which is making particularly fuel and fertilizer scarce and more expensive.

If the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also becomes impassable, the situation could deteriorate further. Shipping companies would have to make detours via the Suez Canal, which is controlled by Egypt or the southern tip of Africa, as some already do. The additional costs would be passed on to consumers.

The human cost of the escalation in Yemen hit Djibouti almost immediately. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), at least 3,700 refugees have crossed from Yemen into Djibouti since September 10. Most of those who made it to the country's northern Obock region are women and children.

The UNHCR is preparing to assist another 10,000 people who have not yet crossed into Djibouti. But Obock, which is on the border with Eritrea, is extremely dry and this is causing other issues.

"We don't have much water here; there's no groundwater at all," Alessandra Roccasalvo, the UN Development Program (UNDP) representative for Djibouti, told DW. "Everything has to be desalinated."

Djibouti is a strategic military hub

Despite its small size, Djibouti — a Muslim-majority Horn of Africa country with a population of just over a million — is a major player in the region. Its position at at the entrance to the Red Sea makes it an attractive commercial and military shipping hub.

The United States, China, France, Italy, and Japan all operate military bases in Djibouti. The German Bundeswehr was also present until 2021, as part of a naval mission to combat maritime piracy.

The country's civilian ports serve as transshipment, or intermediate, hubs for global shipping cargo, goods and containers. So far, the Houthi advance has not led to empty docks in Djibouti.

But there are still potential consequences, said Roccasalvo: "Basically, there's an economic upswing here — which means, as in any country experiencing an upswing, building materials are needed: cement, raw materials, and other things."

Less of that money is now coming in because ships have to pay nearly twice as much for insurance and reinsurance as they used to. "Many ships no longer want to pass through the Suez Canal; many no longer want to pass through the Red Sea."

Knock-on effects for landlocked neighboring Ethiopia

Ethiopia — the world's most populous landlocked country — handles about 95% of its imports and exports through Djibouti's ports. Price hikes resulting from higher war-risk shipping insurance premiums are affecting the country greatly.

Shortly after the Houthis seized Perim, Ethiopia's economy faced another, even more immediate threat: On September 23, fighting broke out in the country's northern Tigray region.

Since then, the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) have reportedly made gains against the Tigray-led rebel coalition that aims to overthrow the national government. The rebels briefly advanced toward the main corridor used for transporting goods between Djibouti's ports and the Ethiopian hinterland.

According to certain experts, the ENDF's advances have since reduced the threat of yet another trade blockade — but as long as the conflict remains unresolved, the situation could potentially deteriorate again.

For months now, Ethiopia has suffered more than almost any other African country from the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and has already had to ration fuel at times. In the long term, the country aims to reduce its dependence on imports, for example by powering vehicles with domestically generated electricity instead of imported gasoline.

Can the conflict in Ethiopia affect Bab el-Mandeb access?

Ethiopia and its northern neighbor, Eritrea, have severed diplomatic ties; other regional powers such as Sudan, Egypt, and Somalia may find themselves siding with Eritrea rather than with Ethiopia.

Eritrea sees itself as facing a threat that Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has reiterated on several occasions: With Ethiopia deprived of access to the sea since Eritrea's independence, Abiy has often alluded to rectifying this perceived injustice — either through a political agreement, as was once sought with Somalia's breakaway region of Somaliland, or by force.

The port of Assab is located on the edge of Eritrea's panhandle — and is often described as the most likely target should Abiy choose the path of aggression. If the fighting within Ethiopia further escalates into a full-blown regional war, this could also lead to additional restrictions on safe passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the surrounding waters.

Experts have also raised concerns about the Shiite Houthis increasingly collaborating with the Sunni terrorist group Al-Shabab, which is based in Somalia. Although their ideologies are fundamentally different, they are particularly united by their hostility toward Israel and the US.

What tools are at the disposal of African countries to help remedy the situation?

The three African non-permanent members of the UN Security Council — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and Somalia — held an emergency meeting in mid-September, jointly calling for free shipping lanes and endorsing the demand that the crisis in Yemen be resolved under the auspices of the UN.

The situation at Bab el-Mandeb and in northern Ethiopia once again demands flexibility from Africa. In fact, some African economies could also benefit from relocation activities: Ports inKenya and Tanzania, for example, are becoming increasingly attractive for transshipment.

And while many countries are suffering from high oil prices, Nigeria's Dangote Group has announced an initial public offering and a new refinery in Kenya.

This article was originally published in German. It has been updated.

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen
